answer:
That name is a genealogy — a chain of who created the face, read innermost outwards. It has three layers, built from the script ([script.js](lab:open?file=script.js&line=17)):

1. **`base.outline.bottom`** — the sketch layer. The sketch is `base`, its rectangle entity is `outline` (from `.rect('outline', …)`), and `bottom` is one of the rect's four sides (`id.bottom right top left`). This is the *source edge* the face was swept from.

2. **`body/side[base.outline.bottom]`** — the extrude layer. The `body` extrude swept the sketch profile up `h`, so the lateral faces it created are `body/side[…]`, and the bracket records which sketch edge each side came from. The two end caps don't need brackets: they're simply `body/end` and `body/start`. [select](lab:face?name=body/side[base.outline.bottom])

3. **`shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]`** — the shell layer. The `shell` feature hollows the box inward, and each inner wall is the offset of an outer wall, so the shell names its inner faces `shell/inner[<the outer face it came from>]`, keeping the whole ancestry in brackets. [select](lab:face?name=shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]])

`why()` confirms this: the resolved chain reads "shell/inner[…] ← shell: offset of body/side[…] ← body: swept from sketch entity base.outline.bottom".

The point of the bracket notation is that the names are **regeneratable from history, not from position**. If you later fillet the vertical corner edges or change `wall`, the bottom-side wall face is still recognisably "the one extruded from `outline.bottom`", so a selector like `j.feat('shell').faces()` filtering on `shell/inner[…bottom…]` keeps pointing at the same intent. If a later feature splits that face, it keeps the name with a `#a`/`#b` suffix instead of becoming `face.17`. Compare that to index-based picks (`.nth(i)`), which raise `ref.fragile` precisely because they don't survive edits.

On its side, flat — the compiler chose **−Y** for the build direction ([open](lab:node?id=cable-clip)). Concretely:

- The clip is one extrusion of the side profile along `w` (12 mm). With the extrusion direction lying along Y on the bed, the whole 12 mm height is one clean stack, and every overhang in the profile (the jaw lead-ins, the channel lip) is a shallow slope that needs no support. The decision record shows **0 mm³ of support**, 240 mm² bed contact and a 12 mm height, versus e.g. printing on the jaw face (+Z), which would need ~1510 mm³ of support under the cable channel and stand 35 mm tall.

The comment in the script ([script.js, near the bottom](lab:open?file=script.js&find=Printed+on+its+side)) says it plainly: the outline lies on the bed, so the layers run along the jaws and the spine, and the clip bends **with** the layer lines rather than across them. That's the real reason this shape wants side-printing: the grip bumps pinch an 18 mm board, so the jaws flex on every push-on; layer lines crossing the spine would put the weak Z-strength exactly where the stress is.

A tie between −Y and +Y exists (same numbers); −Y wins only by lexicographic order. Nothing about the design cares which of the two — both are fine.

One full turn of the pinion moves the rack by the pinion's **circumference at the pitch circle**:

$$\text{travel} = \pi \, m \, z = \pi \times 2 \times 18 = 113.097 \text{ mm}$$

That's the pitch radius $r = \tfrac{mz}{2} = 18$ mm, times $2\pi$ — exactly the coupling rule in the script's own rules (`travel = r × angle`), with angle = one full turn. The rack here is 100 mm long, so one revolution would drive it just past its full 100 mm stroke (~113 mm available at the pitch line); the joint limits presumably stop it short.

You can verify with the mesh inspector — `j.inspect.gearMesh(pinion, rack)` reports the pitch radius and centre distance, and the sweep of the slider joint per turn of the revolute should come out at $2\pi r$.

Reading it from the [front view](lab:view?name=front) (the working profile, drawn on XZ), the outline is a **C-shaped hook with a two-jaw mouth** — one closed polygon that does four jobs:

- **The spine** — the tall back (at $x = -t$, from $z = -2t - \text{cable}$ up to $\text{desk} + t$) is the leaf spring: it spans between the two jaws and provides the flex that lets the clip push on and hold.
- **The top jaw** — the horizontal arm reaching onto the desk ($z = \text{desk}$ to $\text{desk} + t$), ending in the **grip bump** at $\text{desk} - \text{grip}$: it clamps the desk's top face with the 0.6 mm pinch, and its tip has a 1 mm **lead-in ramp** so the desk edge pushes the jaw open as you press the clip on.
- **The bottom jaw** — the mirror of the top one under the desk's underside ($z = -t$ to $0$), with the same grip bump and lead-in at its tip. Together the two jaws sandwich the 18 mm board with grip on both faces.
- **The cable channel** — the lower right pocket ($\text{cable}$ wide, from $-t$ down to $-t - \text{cable}$): the hook that hangs below the bottom jaw, with a step/lip at $\text{cable} + t$ so cables of a few mm sit in the open channel and can't slide off the ends — they slide in along the desk edge.

The [side view](lab:view?name=side) shows why the flat profile matters: printed on its side, the layers run along the length of the spine and jaws, so the spring flexes along layer lines rather than between them.

The name is assembled by **genealogy**: each feature records where its faces came from, so the name reads right-to-left as a history. Here's the chain for this exact part.

**`base.outline.bottom` — the sketch curve.** The sketch `base` is a `rect('outline', 'w', 'd', { center: true, r: 'r' })` ([open](lab:open?file=script.js&find=outline)). A `rect` names its four straight sides `outline.bottom right top left` and its four rounded corners `outline.bl br tr tl`. I checked the solved sketch: `outline.bottom` is the line from `[-27, -20]` to `[27, -20]` — the −Y edge, shortened to ±27 mm by the 3 mm corner radius. That is the source curve.

**`body/side[base.outline.bottom]` — the extrude face.** The `.extrude(…, 'h', { id: 'body' })` pulls that profile up 30 mm. Every sketch edge swept into a side wall, and the wall grown from `outline.bottom` is named by prepending the feature and the role: `body/side[base.outline.bottom]`. The `[…]` bracket always holds *the source curve or face that this face was generated from*. This one is the outer +Y-more-negative wall — the face at $y=-20$, area $30\times(60-2r)+$ corners… measuring it confirms a plane at `y = −20`.

**`shell/inner[…]` — the shell face.** `.shell(j.feat('body').endFace(), 'wall', { direction: 'in', id: 'shell' })` ([open](lab:open?file=script.js&find=shell)) hollows the box, offsetting every wall inward by `wall` = 2 mm and leaving the `body/end` (top) open. answer:
**3 mm walls make the shell feature fail.** Checked with `check()` variants of the untouched file, so nothing in the editor changed:

- `wall = 2.95 mm` → ok, volume 21866.18 mm³, 27.11 g
- `wall = 3 mm` → **error** at line 25, `feature.failed` on `shell`: *"shell of body1 by 3 mm failed (OpenCascade could not offset the faces)"* — fix suggests "reduce the thickness or remove small fillets first"
- `wall = 5 mm` → same error

**Why:** the outline is a rounded rect with `r = 3` ([script.js:21](lab:open?file=script.js&line=21)) and the shell offsets inward ([line 25](lab:open?file=script.js&line=25)). At a convex corner, the inner surface of a `t`-thick shell is an arc of radius $r - t$. At $t = 3 = r$ that radius goes to zero: the two inner walls become tangent to each other and the offset collapses into a degenerate, non-offsettable corner, so the kernel gives up. The condition is strictly $r > t$ — `r = 3.01` with `wall = 3` compiles fine, and so does the whole range below 3.

I confirmed it's the corner radius and nothing else:

| variant | volume | mass |
|---|---|---|
| wall 3, r 3 (default) | — shell fails | — |
| wall 3, r 4 | 22039.14 mm³ | 27.33 g |
| wall 3, r 0 (sharp corners) | 22428 mm³ | 27.81 g |
| wall 5, r 0 | 34500 mm³ | — |

Those agree with the closed form: outer $2400 - (4-\pi)r^2$ × 30 mm, minus the cavity $54 \times 34$ with corner radius $r-t$ × 27 mm. Only the corner arcs are involved — the small `r = 0.5` case fails at every thickness too, since $r < t$ holds there as well.

**So if you want 3 mm walls**, the three working options are: raise the corner radius above the wall (`r: mm(4)` or more), square the corners (`r: mm(0)`), or keep the wall just under the radius (2.95 mm works, 27.11 g). Note `wall` has a slider range up to 5 mm in `.expose`, so the failing zone (3 mm … 5 mm at the default `r = 3`) is reachable from the Params view — a [param link](lab:param?name=wall&value=3 mm) will show the error in Diagnostics rather than a broken model. If you like, I can edit line 21 to make `r` a function of `wall` (e.g. `r: 'max(3, wall + 1)'`) so any thickness in range stays valid.

**Done — the outline sketch is now fully constrained, 0 DOF, no `sketch.underConstrained` warning** (the compile reports `warnings: 0`, diagnostics empty, volume still 12672.7655 mm³ exact, mass 15.714 g).

The count, as the solver sees it: before the change the sketch had $2\cdot3 + 4\cdot4 = 22$ entity DOF (two circles at 3 each, four lines at 4 each), and the constraint rows — 4 implicit `coincident` (8), `fix` (2), 2 `horizontal` + 2 `vertical` (4), `equal` (1), and 6 dimensions (6) — gave $\operatorname{rank} J = 21$. So $\text{DOF} = 22 - 21 = 1$, and the free coordinate was exactly `h2:center.x`. One horizontal distance adds one independent row (the x-difference of two centres), so $\operatorname{rank} J = 22$ and DOF $=0$.

I followed the brief and tied the dimension to a param rather than typing 48 into the slot — [script.js line 26](lab:open?file=script.js&line=26):

```js
.dim({ h: ['h1.center', 'h2.center'] }, 'hole_pitch')   // with hole_pitch: mm(48) in .params

Dragging on the sheet now moves nothing — the handle you used to slide is gone.

Two notes for you. The reference is `h1.center`, so `h2` tracks the left edge, not the right: at `w` = 120 mm ([lab:param](lab:param?name=w&value=120%20mm)) it sits 60 mm from each side only by coincidence — the right margin grows with `w`. If you want a symmetric plate, use `.dim({ h: ['h2.center', 'l2.start'] }, 'edge')` instead (the suggestion that used to be in the notes). I also updated [notes.md](lab:open?file=notes.md&line=15), which still claimed 1 DOF and a draggable `h2`. Optionally add `hole_pitch` to `.expose([...])` so it becomes a slider next to `w`, `d` and `hole_d`.

**On its side — build direction `−Y`, so the side-profile outline lies flat on the bed and the 12 mm clip width is the print height.**

The print job's orientation decision ([script.js:66](lab:open?file=script.js&line=66)) says it plainly: `lexicographic: support 0 mm³ → bed contact 240 mm² → height 12.0 mm (next: +Y, support 0 mm³)`. The bed face is one of the two flat side faces, `body/end` at 240.4 mm² (exact B-rep), which is the C-shaped outline — the same profile the sketch draws on XZ. Height 12 mm is exactly `w`, i.e. the extrude depth, so the job is 60 layers of 0.2 mm, 12.1 min, 1.091 m of filament, ~3.66 g in PETG.

Why the automatic pick won, against the five alternatives the compiler tried:

| build dir | support | bed contact | height |
|---|---|---|---|
| **−Y / +Y** (on its side) | **0 mm³** | 240 mm² | **12 mm** |
| +X (on its back) | 134 mm³ | 420 mm² | 18 mm |
| −Z (upright) | 1451 mm³ | 216 mm² | 35 mm |
| +Z (upright) | 1510 mm³ | 168 mm² | 35 mm |
| −X | 1638 mm³ | 48 mm² | 18 mm |

The rule is lexicographic and support-first, so the two zero-support poses beat everything else before bed contact or height is even consulted; ±Y tie on all three numbers and the first listed wins. `+X` has more bed contact but needs 134 mm³ of support (the jaws and spine overhang), and standing the clip up on its 18 × 35 silhouette would need ~1.5 cm³ of support under the whole jaw/channel undercut.

The engineering reason it's also the right answer: every layer is a copy of the outline, so the spine and both jaws are stacks of identical contours and the layer planes cross the 12 mm width only. When a jaw flexes open (in Z, as the 0.6 mm grip bumps ride over the desk edge) the tensile stress runs *along* the jaw and spine, in-plane — never peeling a layer off its neighbour. Nothing in the profile is an overhang either: `overhang: []`, support volume 0, the cable channel's inner walls and the jaw lead-ins all print as vertical contour, not as bridges.

The one thing to watch is that the tie between ±Y is arbitrary — flipping it changes which flat face is on the bed but nothing else, so a `.orient('+Y')` would be equally good. If you widen `w` you pay in layers, not in support: `lab:param?name=w&value=30 mm` gives the same footprint at 150 layers.

It reads as a **C-clamp with a hook under it**: five params ($desk=18$, $cable=8$, $t=3$, $jaw=15$, $grip=0.6$ mm) place every vertex, and the result is an 18 × 12 × 35 mm block silhouette of material, 2884.8 mm³ (exact B-rep).

- **Spine** — the vertical bar at $x=-t\ldots0$, running the full 35 mm height. It sits just outboard of the board's edge and is the only piece outside the desk's footprint; it ties the top jaw, bottom jaw and cable hook together.
- **Top jaw** — a 3 mm arm at $z=desk\ldots desk+t$ reaching in to $x=jaw=15$. Its tip is a small step (down to $z=desk+1$) and then a 2 mm lead-in ramp from $(13,\ desk-grip)$ to the tip, so the mouth opens as the clip is pushed on.
- **Bottom jaw** — the mirror arm at $z=-t\ldots0$, tip at $z=-1$ with the same ramp up to the bump at $(13,\ +grip)$.
- **Grip bumps** — the two short segments at $x=jaw-4\ldots jaw-2$: 0.6 mm proud of 18 mm, so the $16.8$ mm pinch between them is 0.6 mm of interference per side — the whole grip of the clip.
- **The board seat** — the two 18 mm-long flats at $z=0$ and $z=desk$ ($x=0\ldots jaw-4$) and the 18 mm vertical at $x=0$: these three faces only touch the board, they don't grip.
- **Cable hook below the bottom jaw** — the spine continues down past the 3 mm jaw to $z=-2t-cable=-14$ and turns right into an 11 mm foot (the floor). A 3 mm lip rises at $x=cable\ldots cable+t$ to $z=-t-cable/2=-7$, halving the mouth: the channel is 8 × 8 mm internally (x 0…8, z −11…−3) but opens only 4 mm high, so a cable snaps past the lip and stays put. Read top to bottom the outline is: **jaw arm → spine → foot → lip → channel floor → channel back → bottom jaw → lead-in → grip bump → board seat → desk edge → seat → grip bump → lead-in → tip**.
